server/index.js.overview: The backend entry point for Curam Vault. It builds the Express app, mounts middleware in a deliberate order (request context, public embeddable routes, helmet, key-authenticated ingest routes, body parsers), then puts `requireAuth` in front of every remaining `/api` router and gates most of them with per-feature flags and an AI rate limiter. In production it also serves the built React SPA. Finally `start()` waits for the database schema, seeds an initial admin, starts cron jobs and opens the HTTP server with a WebSocket attachment. This is the hub file for tour step 1.

sections.title: Bootstrap and encryption check
sections.explanation: Environment variables load first, then Sentry is required before anything else so it can instrument `http`, `express` and `pg` automatically. A guarded check warns when the Gmail token encryption key is missing, but exits the process if the key exists and is malformed, because a broken key would corrupt stored tokens. `trust proxy` is set to 1 so the rate limiter sees the real client IP behind Railway's proxy.

sections.title: Request context and public widgets
sections.explanation: `requestContext` and `httpLogger` are mounted before everything else so even requests that helmet or a limiter rejects still get a request id and a log line. The Cellar Planner LITE routes come next: they are public, embeddable in a business's own website, and set their own headers, so they must sit before helmet and before `requireAuth`. Routers are built by factory functions that receive the shared `pool`, which keeps them testable.

sections.title: Helmet Content Security Policy
sections.explanation: In production helmet applies a CSP that extends the defaults. Each relaxation is documented inline with the feature that needs it: `wasm-unsafe-eval` and `blob:` for @react-pdf, `data:` in `connect-src` for pdfjs, specific image hosts for Garden Planner photos and MapTiler, and `blob:` frames for Finance receipt previews. In development CSP is turned off entirely (`false`), so CSP bugs only show up in production builds.

sections.title: Key-auth ingest and body parsers
sections.explanation: The Vault Shelf and Ponytail ingest routes authenticate with their own keys, so they go before `requireAuth`, and also before the 30 MB JSON parser on purpose: the router checks the key before reading a much smaller body. After that, a large-request logger and the generous JSON/urlencoded parsers are mounted, the upload directory is created if missing, and requiring `./db` kicks off connection and schema creation as a side effect.

sections.title: Initial admin seeding
sections.explanation: `seedInitialUser` creates the first admin from seed credentials in environment variables, but only when the `users` table is empty, so it is safe to run on every boot. The password is hashed with bcrypt at cost 12 before insert, and the email is lower-cased to match the login lookup.

sections.title: Public routes before the auth gate
sections.explanation: Auth, shared-task previews, OAuth callbacks (Gmail, Search Console, Calendar) and several token-proven endpoints (fitness unsubscribe, the PC Health helper, inbound burner mail, the Live TV player frame) are mounted here. Each one either needs no login or proves itself with its own secret or token, and the comments explain why each is safe to leave public.

sections.title: Auth gate and feature routers
sections.explanation: `app.use('/api', requireAuth)` makes every later `/api` route authenticated. Routers are then mounted with `requireFeature(key)` (per-member toggles), `requireAdmin` for admin-only tools, and `aiLimiter` on endpoints that call paid model APIs. Order matters: more specific prefixes such as `/api/shares/news` are registered before `/api/shares` so prefix matching does not swallow them. Some routers apply the limiter internally (music, translate via `aiLimiterExcept`) because polling GETs would otherwise burn the per-user AI budget.

sections.title: SPA serving and error handling
sections.explanation: In production the built `dist` folder is served statically, with a catch-all that returns `index.html` so client-side routes work on refresh. Sentry's Express error handler is placed after all routes, followed by a final JSON error handler that logs through the request-scoped logger. Process-level handlers log fatal errors; on an uncaught exception the code flushes Sentry for up to two seconds before exiting, because `captureException` only enqueues.

sections.title: Startup sequence and cron jobs
sections.explanation: `start()` polls `SELECT 1 FROM users` up to ten times because `db.js` runs `initSchema` asynchronously on require, so the server must wait until tables exist. It then seeds the admin, runs best-effort backfills and starts crons in two groups: jobs that send nothing run everywhere, while jobs that call external services are skipped when `disableExternalCron` is set (for staging). The API key presence check logs a short prefix of each configured key; this is convenient for debugging but means a few characters of each secret end up in logs.

sections.title: Enum drift check and listen
sections.explanation: The Contract Review block compares `CONTRACT_TYPE_KEYS` exported by `db.js` with the playbook keys and, on mismatch, files a Suggestions alert for the admin instead of exiting; the comment explains that an earlier `process.exit(1)` took the whole app down for a single-feature drift. Finally a plain `http` server wraps the Express app so the browser-agent WebSocket can attach to the same port. The app is exported for tests.

client/src/main.jsx.overview: The frontend entry point that Vite loads. It creates a React 18 root on the `#root` element, imports the global stylesheet and renders `App` inside `React.StrictMode`. Everything else on the client starts from `App.jsx`, covered in tour step 1.

sections.title: React root mount
sections.explanation: `createRoot` from `react-dom/client` is the React 18 API that enables concurrent rendering. `StrictMode` double-invokes effects in development, which helps catch effects that lack cleanup (many effects in `App` and `Layout` register and remove event listeners for this reason). The global `index.css` (Tailwind) is imported once here so every page shares it.

client/src/App.jsx.overview: The root React component. It wraps the app in theme and icon providers, sets up global keyboard shortcuts and declares the full route tree: public routes (login, password reset, shared tasks) and an `AuthGuard`-protected `Layout` route under which every workspace page renders. It also decides where a user lands after signing in. Tour step 1 introduces it as the client-side counterpart to `server/index.js`.

sections.title: Page and shell imports
sections.explanation: Every page is imported eagerly, so the main bundle contains all tools; only heavy editors such as Excalidraw are loaded lazily inside their pages, as the comment on the Drawings import notes. Providers, `Layout`, `FeatureRoute`, `AuthGuard`, global modals and `useAuthStore` round out the dependencies.

sections.title: Landing and admin routes
sections.explanation: `HomeRoute` picks the start page: accountant logins always go to `/finance`, an admin-configured landing path or external link is honoured once per sign-in per tab (tracked in `sessionStorage` keyed by token, wrapped in try/catch for private windows), narrow screens get the mobile dashboard, and everyone else gets `ProjectList`. `AdminRoute` is a client-side convenience redirect only; the real enforcement is `requireAdmin` on the server.

sections.title: Global keyboard shortcuts
sections.explanation: A single `keydown` listener handles Ctrl/Cmd shortcuts: `/` toggles the shortcuts modal, `B` dispatches a `vault:toggle-sidebar` custom event that `Layout` listens for, and `N` opens the new-chat modal, defaulting to the current project when the URL matches `/projects/:id/chat`. Using DOM custom events avoids threading state between `App` and `Layout`.

sections.title: Provider stack and route tree
sections.explanation: `ThemeProvider` and `IconProvider` wrap the router so every page can call `useIcon`. Global overlays (search palette, processing modal, new-chat host) render outside `Routes`. The protected section uses a layout route, `<AuthGuard><Layout /></AuthGuard>`, so pages render in Layout's `<Outlet />`; nested student-quiz routes show the same pattern one level down. `FeatureRoute` gates a page by feature flag on the client, while unknown paths redirect to `/`.

package.json.overview: The single manifest for both halves of the project: one Express server and one Vite/React client share one `package.json`. It defines dev, build and start scripts, a long list of per-feature test scripts that run plain Node test files, and the runtime dependencies (Anthropic and Gemini SDKs, Express, pg, Playwright, document and image libraries). Tour step 1 points to it as the glue between server and client.

sections.title: Metadata and lifecycle scripts
sections.explanation: `main` points to `server/index.js`. `dev` runs the nodemon server and Vite client in parallel with `concurrently`; `build` runs the Vite build and then several Node scripts that build the separate planner bundles (room, garden and others); `start` runs the server alone, which serves the built `dist` in production. `migrate:embeddings` is a one-off maintenance script.

sections.title: Per-feature test scripts
sections.explanation: There is no test framework: each `test:*` script runs one or more `.test.js` or `.test.mjs` files directly with `node`, chained with `&&`. Server tests live next to the code they test, and client utility tests use `.mjs` so Node can load them as ES modules without a bundler. A few `--live` and `.probe.js` scripts call real external services and are kept separate from the offline tests.

sections.title: Runtime dependencies
sections.explanation: The server stack is `express`, `helmet`, `express-rate-limit`, `pg`, `pino`, `@sentry/node` and `node-cron`. AI access goes through `@anthropic-ai/sdk` and `@google/generative-ai`. Many libraries support document tools (pdf-lib, pdfjs-dist, mammoth, xlsx, pptxgenjs, tesseract.js, sharp), and `playwright` plus `ws` power the browser agent. Some client libraries (Excalidraw, Tiptap, Recharts) are listed here too.

sections.title: Build-time and client dependencies
sections.explanation: React, React Router, Zustand, Tailwind, lucide-react and Vite are devDependencies because Vite bundles them into `dist` at build time and the production server never requires them. That only works because the build runs where devDependencies are installed, which matters for deployment configuration.

server/db.js.overview: The PostgreSQL foundation of the server and its most depended-upon file. It creates a single `pg` Pool, wraps `pool.query` and `pool.connect` so every query gets slow-query and failure logging, and defines one very large `initSchema` function that creates and migrates every table, index and seed row. Requiring the module connects and runs `initSchema` straight away, which is why `index.js` polls until tables exist. All DDL is idempotent so it can run on every boot (tour step 2).

sections.title: Pool and SSL configuration
sections.explanation: `sslConfig` turns SSL on for any non-localhost database URL and sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`, which suits hosted providers with self-signed chains but skips certificate verification. The pool allows 10 connections with a 30 s idle and 10 s connect timeout. The connection string comes from `runtimeConfig`, not straight from `process.env`.

sections.title: Traced query wrapper
sections.explanation: `tracedQueryFn` wraps a query function so failures and queries over 200 ms are logged through `getLogger()`, which means log lines carry the current request id and user id. The long comment explains a real bug: pg-pool calls `client.query(text, values, callback)` internally, so the wrapper must detect a trailing callback and keep it; an earlier version dropped it and the app hung on boot. Replacing `pool.query` in place gives every existing call site tracing without code changes.

sections.title: Transaction client patching
sections.explanation: Transactions use `pool.connect()` and then `client.query`, which bypassed the wrapper. `tracedConnect` supports both the promise style used by app code and the callback style pg-pool uses internally for `pool.query`, and `patchClient` marks clients with `__traced` so pooled clients that come back are not wrapped twice.

sections.title: Contract Review enum keys
sections.explanation: `CONTRACT_TYPE_KEYS` and `PARTY_ROLE_KEYS` are the single source of truth for two CHECK constraints. They are interpolated into the migration SQL and exported so `index.js` can compare them with the playbook keys at startup, avoiding two hand-maintained lists that drift apart.

sections.title: Transactional core schema
sections.explanation: `initSchema` first records the database clock (used to tell earlier processes' jobs apart), then opens one transaction and runs a long series of `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` statements for the core tables. Everything commits together or rolls back on error, and the client is always released in `finally`. Because it runs on every boot, every statement must be idempotent.

sections.title: Post-commit FKs and pgvector
sections.explanation: Work that may fail on some hosts runs outside the transaction and in separate try/catch blocks: forward-reference foreign keys, knowledge-graph edges, and the RAG setup (`CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector` plus a `file_chunks` table for 768-dimension embeddings). If pgvector is not installed, a warning is logged and the server still starts with RAG disabled.

sections.title: Multi-user and feature migrations
sections.explanation: This region adds columns to existing tables with `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`: admin flags, `featureOverrides` (which can only turn features off for a member), accountant links, access expiry and landing paths, then per-user columns and tables for usage logs, mood, CRM audit logs and backfills, mission statements, shares and dividends. The file contains about 240 such additive migrations, which is how the schema evolves without a migration tool.

sections.title: Feature-specific schema blocks
sections.explanation: Tables for later features are grouped under banner comments: admin changelog and nav seeds, Ponytail report, shares thesis, metals, YouTube, many Finance additions (recurring items, drawings, budgets, audit log, bills, BAS, document library), Translate, translation memory, Guitar and Contract Review. Contract Review constraints use the enum arrays defined at the top of the file.

sections.title: Seeds and data migrations
sections.explanation: Clause-type seed rows are inserted with `ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING` so repeat boots add nothing. The fitness library seed and the garden picture migration each sit in their own try/catch and log 'will retry next boot' on failure, so an optional data step can never block startup.

sections.title: Startup side effect and exports
sections.explanation: On first require the module runs `SELECT NOW()` and then `initSchema()`, exiting the process if either fails. This is a side effect at import time: any script that requires `db.js` triggers schema setup. The exports are the traced `pool`, `initSchema` and the two enum arrays.

server/middleware/auth.js.overview: The authentication and authorisation middleware used by `server/index.js`. `requireAuth` validates a bearer session token against the `auth_sessions` table and loads the user; `requireAdmin` gates admin routes; `requireFeature` and `requireAnyFeature` enforce per-member feature flags built from workspace settings and user overrides, including the special accountant scope. This is the gate described in tour step 3.

sections.title: Dependencies
sections.explanation: The middleware reads the database through the shared `pool`, uses the feature-access config helpers to compute flags, attaches the user id to the request log context, and delegates accountant handling to `applyAccountantScope`.

sections.title: requireAuth session check
sections.explanation: Although the tour mentions JWTs, this code uses opaque session tokens: it takes the `Bearer` token, looks it up in `auth_sessions`, and deletes expired sessions on the spot. `/health` and `/auth/*` are skipped because the middleware is mounted on all of `/api`. Disabled users are rejected unless they are accountant logins. A throttled fire-and-forget `lastActiveAt` update never blocks the request. `applyAccountantScope` sets `req.user` (and can end the response itself), after which the user id is attached to the logger.

sections.title: requireAdmin guard
sections.explanation: A simple synchronous guard that returns 401 without a user and 403 for non-admins. It assumes `requireAuth` already ran, which the global `app.use('/api', requireAuth)` in `index.js` guarantees.

sections.title: Loading feature flags
sections.explanation: `loadFeatureAccess` reads every `feature_%` row in `workspace_settings`, then narrows them with the user's `featureOverrides`. Accountant users get a fixed flag set from `accountantFlags`. It runs two queries per guarded request and has no cache, which keeps toggles instant at the cost of extra database reads.

sections.title: requireFeature factory
sections.explanation: Returns middleware for one feature key. Unknown keys pass through and admins always pass. Only an explicit `false` blocks, so features default to on. For accountants, `req.featureUserId` holds the accountant's own id while `req.user.id` is the owner's id, so flags come from the right account while data reads come from the owner's.

sections.title: requireAnyFeature and exports
sections.explanation: For shared services such as geocoding used by several tools, this guard blocks only when every listed feature is off. Note that it uses `req.user?.id` rather than `req.featureUserId`, unlike `requireFeature`. `loadFeatureAccess` is exported too so routes can report flags to the client.

server/middleware/requestContext.js.overview: Gives every request a correlation id and a request-scoped pino child logger stored in Node's `AsyncLocalStorage`. Any code running during the request, including the database wrapper in `db.js`, can call `getLogger()` to log with the request id and, after authentication, the user id. It is mounted first in `index.js` and is the tracing half of tour step 3.

sections.title: Imports and async storage
sections.explanation: One module-level `AsyncLocalStorage` instance holds the per-request store. `randomUUID` from `crypto` creates ids without extra dependencies, and the base pino logger comes from `lib/logger`.

sections.title: requestContext middleware
sections.explanation: It reuses an incoming `x-request-id` header when there is one (useful behind a proxy) or creates a UUID, echoes it in the response header, sets `req.requestId`, and runs `next()` inside `als.run`. Everything later in the middleware chain, including awaited code, then sees the same store.

sections.title: Attaching the user
sections.explanation: `requireAuth` calls this once the user is known. It replaces the store's logger with a child that also carries `userId`. Changing the store in place works because the store object is shared by the rest of the request's async chain.

sections.title: getLogger and exports
sections.explanation: `getLogger` returns the request-scoped logger inside a request and falls back to the base logger at startup or in cron jobs. Because of this fallback, shared code such as `db.js` can call it anywhere without checking for a request first.

client/src/utils/apiClient.js.overview: The single HTTP wrapper every page uses to call `/api`. It adds the bearer token from `authStore`, clears auth and redirects to `/login` on any 401, and offers helpers for JSON verbs, multipart uploads, safe file downloads and streaming responses. Most methods return the raw `Response`, so callers call `.json()` themselves. It is the centre of tour step 4.

sections.title: CRM follow-up side channel
sections.explanation: Because every task update already goes through `api.put`, this is the one place that can react when a CRM-linked task is completed from any of about 20 screens. On a successful `PUT /api/tasks/:id`, it reads a cloned response (so the caller's body is untouched) and, if the server included `crmFollowUp`, shows a toast with a link to log the outcome. Errors are swallowed on purpose so this side channel never breaks the real request.

sections.title: Headers and 401 handling
sections.explanation: `getHeaders` reads the token with `useAuthStore.getState()`, the way to read Zustand outside React components. `handleResponse` treats any 401 as a lost session: it clears auth, does a full redirect to `/login` and throws, so callers never handle expired sessions themselves. Other error statuses are passed back to the caller.

sections.title: JSON verbs and form uploads
sections.explanation: `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch` and `delete` send JSON and accept an optional `AbortSignal`; `patch` and `delete` send a body only when one is given. `postForm` leaves out `Content-Type` so the browser can set the multipart boundary itself, a common mistake the comment warns about.

sections.title: Safe binary download
sections.explanation: `download` checks status and content type before saving, so a JSON error is never saved as a `.pdf` or `.docx`. It reads the filename from `Content-Disposition` (including the RFC 5987 `filename*=UTF-8''` form), clicks a temporary object-URL link, and revokes the URL after a short delay so the browser has time to start the download.

sections.title: Streaming requests
sections.explanation: `stream` POSTs JSON and returns the raw `Response` so chat pages can read the server-sent event stream with a reader. It repeats the 401 redirect inline instead of calling `handleResponse`, as `download` does, so the three 401 code paths must be kept in step by hand.

client/src/store/authStore.js.overview: A tiny persisted Zustand store holding the session token and current user. `apiClient` reads the token from it for every request, `App` and `Layout` read the user's flags, and `clearAuth` logs the user out on the client. The `persist` middleware saves it to localStorage under `vault-auth`, so sessions survive reloads (tour step 4).

sections.title: Persisted auth store
sections.explanation: `create(persist(...))` builds a hook-style store with `token`, `user`, `setAuth` and `clearAuth`. Components subscribe to slices (`useAuthStore((s) => s.token)`), while non-React code uses `getState()`. Because the bearer token sits in localStorage, any script running on the page can read it, which is why the strict production CSP in `server/index.js` matters.

client/src/store/toastStore.js.overview: A small Zustand store for short-lived notifications. Any module, including non-React code such as `apiClient`, can call `addToast`; the `Toast` component rendered by `Layout` shows the list. Toasts remove themselves after a timeout and can carry an action link or button (tour step 4).

sections.title: Toast queue with auto-dismiss
sections.explanation: A module-level counter gives each toast a unique id. `addToast` appends the toast and schedules its removal; the default time is 5 s, or 10 s when there is an action to click, a choice the comment ties to WCAG 2.2.1 (enough time). Actions can be `{ label, href }` or `{ label, onClick }`, for example Undo. `removeToast` lets the user close one early; the timer then filters out an id that is already gone, which is harmless.

client/src/components/Layout.jsx.overview: The app shell every signed-in page renders inside, through React Router's `<Outlet />`. It manages the resizable sidebar, the top bar with breadcrumb and quick links, mobile navigation, a staging banner, and a set of popups (due-today banner, task reminders, morning digest, reflection reminder). On mount it loads feature-access flags, environment info and badge counts through `apiClient`. Tour step 5 describes it as the frame around all tools.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: The shell brings in the sidebar, toolbars, popups and launchers, plus `useIcon`, `authStore`, `settingsStore` and `apiClient`. Navigation metadata (`TOP_BAR_LINKS`, `trailForPath`) comes from a config module, and `DEFAULT_FEATURE_ACCESS` provides fallback flags before the server answers.

sections.title: Sidebar state and drag-resize
sections.explanation: The sidebar starts closed on mobile and uses a saved preference on desktop; its width is limited to 180-520 px. Resizing uses refs (`isResizing`, start X and width) and global mouse listeners in an effect, so dragging does not re-render on every pixel through state and keeps working when the pointer leaves the handle.

sections.title: Popup state and initial data
sections.explanation: Several state slots drive banners and badges. Effects run once to fetch tasks due today (unless dismissed for the session), bookmark and suggestion counts (refreshed on `vault:*-changed` window events), feature-access flags merged over the defaults, environment info for the staging banner, and mission-reminder status. Every fetch ends in `.catch(() => {})`, so a failed side request never breaks the shell.

sections.title: Reflection and task reminders
sections.explanation: The reflection (inquiry) reminder is checked on mount and again on route change in case a new day has started, and it waits its turn behind other popups through `usePopupSlot`. Task reminders show the most recent missed reminder from the last four hours on mount, then check every minute against the user's reminder times unless reminders are paused.

sections.title: Responsiveness, logout and gating
sections.explanation: Effects track the mobile breakpoint, close the sidebar after navigation on mobile, and listen for the `vault:toggle-sidebar` event sent by `App`'s shortcut. `handleLogout` tells the server, then clears local auth even if that call fails. `canUseFeature` mirrors the server rule (admins always pass, only explicit `false` blocks). Section visits are counted at most once per section every 30 minutes for admin usage stats.

sections.title: Top bar links and sidebar styles
sections.explanation: `renderTopBarLink` draws one quick link from `TOP_BAR_LINKS` with its icon from `getIcon`, and highlights it for the whole section with `isNavItemActive`. The sidebar style switches between a fixed overlay on mobile and a push layout with the saved width on desktop.

sections.title: Shell markup: banner, sidebar, top bar
sections.explanation: The render starts with an optional staging banner and reduces the shell height by its 26 px so nothing is pushed off screen. It then lays out the mobile backdrop, `ProjectSidebar` with its desktop drag handle, and the top bar containing the Group > Page breadcrumb, quick links, launchers and mobile-only controls.

sections.title: Page outlet and overlays
sections.explanation: Below the top bar come the mobile nav dropdown, the due-today banner and the scrollable `<main>` holding `<Outlet />`, where the routed page renders. Global overlays follow outside the main column: `Toast`, `MorningDigest`, `TaskReminderModal`, the reflection reminder banner and `InquirySession`, so they stay visible on every page.

client/src/providers/IconProvider.jsx.overview: A React context that gives components a `getIcon(name, props)` function through the `useIcon` hook. Semantic names such as 'settings' or 'delete' are looked up in `iconMap`'s `semanticMap` and rendered as lucide-react components, so components never import icon libraries directly. Its wide use across components is why tour step 5 highlights it.

sections.title: Imports and context
sections.explanation: The whole `lucide-react` namespace is imported so icons can be looked up by string name at runtime. The trade-off is that tree-shaking cannot remove unused icons from the bundle. The context starts as `null`, so `useIcon` outside the provider returns `null`.

sections.title: IconProvider resolver
sections.explanation: `getIcon` maps a semantic name to `mapping.lucide`, finds the component and renders it at a default size of 18, which callers can override with props. Unknown names return `null` instead of throwing. The memo depends on the `iconPack` setting, but the resolver currently always reads the `lucide` entry, so changing the pack only creates a new function; other packs would need a branch added here.

sections.title: useIcon hook and exports
sections.explanation: `useIcon` is a thin `useContext` wrapper, and the provider is exported both by name (as `App.jsx` imports it) and as the default export.

client/src/utils/featureAccess.js.overview: The client-side copy of the per-member feature flags. It defines the default on/off state of every tool, how finished each tool is (preview or parked), and the grouped labels the admin settings screen uses to show the toggles. Layout.jsx and the routing use these defaults alongside the user's stored access, and the server enforces the same keys (Step 3), so this file has to stay in step with server/config/featureAccess.js.

sections.title: Default feature access
sections.explanation: `DEFAULT_FEATURE_ACCESS` maps each tool key to whether a member gets it when nothing is stored for them. Most tools default to `true`; unfinished or sensitive ones such as `passwordVault`, `liveTv` and `shelf` default to `false`. Several comments say `keep in step with server/config/featureAccess.js`: the client only uses these values to hide UI, while the server's copy is the real gate, so the two must not drift apart.

sections.title: Lifecycle labels
sections.explanation: `FEATURE_LIFECYCLE` marks tools as `preview` or `parked`; a key that is missing counts as generally available (`ga`). `LIFECYCLE_LABELS` holds the badge text and tooltip for each state. The comment notes that a test fails if this table differs from the server copy, which is how the duplication is kept safe.

sections.title: Grouped toggle options
sections.explanation: `FEATURE_ACCESS_GROUPS` arranges the same keys into 'Website' and 'Apps' groups with human labels for the settings UI. `FEATURE_ACCESS_OPTIONS` flattens the groups with `flatMap`, so code that just needs every key and label does not have to walk the groups. Labels can differ from keys (for example `productScout` is shown as 'Amazon Search'), so the UI should always read labels from here.

client/src/pages/NotesPage.jsx.overview: The Notes workspace page and the largest example of how a Vault tool page is built. It owns the open note's state, a serialized autosave queue, dictation, templates, saved views, tags, attachments, reminders, AI actions and version history, and hands the list and most dialogs to smaller components under pages/notes. All server calls go through apiClient (Step 4) to routes/notes.js, and the Tiptap rich editor is lazy-loaded so it only downloads when Rich mode is first used (Step 6).

sections.title: Imports and lazy editor
sections.explanation: The page imports apiClient, the icon hook, Zustand stores and about thirty helpers and panels from `./notes/`, which keeps this file focused on coordination. Constants set the autosave pause (`AUTOSAVE_DELAY = 1000` ms) and the localStorage key for the editor mode. `RichNoteEditor` is created with `lazy(() => import(...))`, so Tiptap becomes a separate bundle chunk fetched only when someone picks Rich.

sections.title: Page state and refs
sections.explanation: `useNotesList` owns the list and its filters; this component holds the open note. The comment explains a key design choice: `selected` holds the note's details while the text lives in separate `title`/`body` state, so typing does not re-render the list. Mirror refs (`selectedRef`, `bodyValueRef`, `titleValueRef`) are kept in sync by effects so async callbacks can read the latest values without stale closures. Many `show...` flags control the dialogs and panels.

sections.title: Serialized autosave
sections.explanation: Only one pending edit is kept, and saves are chained on a single promise (`chain.current`) so a slow PUT can never land after a newer one. `scheduleSave` restarts a one-second timer and keeps a special `versionReason` (for example after an AI change) even if the person keeps typing. On failure the words are put back into `pending` so 'Try again' can resend them. Hiding the tab, `pagehide` and unmounting all flush the save straight away.

sections.title: Dictation and opening notes
sections.explanation: `useDictation` appends recognised speech to the open note, and if the person has switched notes meanwhile it writes the words to the original note through the API instead. `selectNote` flushes any save, resets panels, and loads the full body only when the list row lacks it. A `selectToken` counter discards late responses when the person clicks another note before the first load finishes, a simple guard against race conditions. A `?note=ID` link opens a note once.

sections.title: Creating, templates, delete
sections.explanation: Handlers for new notes, the person's own templates (load, create from, save as, delete), undoing a delete from the recycle bin, voice notes coming back from the recorder, delete, convert to task and 'open as chat'. Deletes go to the recycle bin on the server, so `undoDelete` can restore by `binId` from a toast.

sections.title: Modes, views, tags, files, reminders
sections.explanation: The editor mode (Write, Rich, Preview) is remembered per device, and ticking a to-do in Preview is written back into the text like any edit. Saved views are compared to the current filters to show which view is active or changed. Tags, attachments and reminders are treated as 'filing': saved immediately rather than through the typing pause, rolled back if the save fails, and they leave the note's edited date alone.

sections.title: Tour, deep links, AI, versions
sections.explanation: Query parameters such as `?record=1`, `?new=1` and `?tour=1` open the recorder, a new note or the guided tour. The AI action handlers only run when the person accepts a proposal, and they keep an `aiBackup` for one Undo. Earlier versions save the on-screen text first, and 'Make tasks' turns unticked to-dos into tasks, with the server returning the updated text to show.

sections.title: Filing and typing handlers
sections.explanation: Clients are loaded lazily, and project or client changes are saved at once. Title, textarea and Rich editor changes all funnel into `scheduleSave`. The textarea handler also drives the `@` mention menu, and helpers insert or append text from web, Gmail or Calendar pull-ins. `openGuideTool` lets the Notes guide chat (Step 9) open real controls.

sections.title: Layout derivations
sections.explanation: On a phone the page shows either the list or the open note, never both. Shared style objects use CSS variables such as `var(--color-border)` so the page follows the theme. Mood data for list rows is fetched only on desktop, since moods are shown only on hover.

sections.title: Render tree
sections.explanation: The JSX puts `NotesListPanel` next to the editor area, which switches between a Preview view, the lazy `RichNoteEditor` inside `<Suspense>` with an 'Opening the editor…' fallback, and a plain textarea. Below it, each dialog (recorder, versions, templates, Ask your notes, reminders, recycle bin) is rendered only when its flag is set. `NotesTutorChat` is always mounted as the page's guide.

server/routes/notes.js.overview: The Express router for /api/notes, mounted behind the auth gate (Step 3). It covers the light note list with filters, tags, templates, saved views, 'Ask your notes', voice notes, versions, live to-dos, single-note CRUD, attachments, reminders, pinning, AI actions and recycle-bin deletes. Most logic is delegated to small services (noteQuery, noteAsk, noteVersions, noteTodos, recycleBin), and every query is scoped to `req.user.id`. It is the server half of the Notes tool from Step 6.

sections.title: Imports and limits
sections.explanation: Imports the database pool, the AI rate limiter, ffmpeg helpers, and a set of note services. Some are deliberately called through their module object (`noteAi.runNoteAction`, `noteAsk.askNotes`) so tests can swap them. Constants cap templates, files per note and list size. Recordings use `multer.memoryStorage()` with a 60 MB cap, so audio is held in memory only for the request.

sections.title: List, options and tags
sections.explanation: `GET /` builds its WHERE clause with `noteQuery.buildFilters`, the same helper Ask uses, so 'the notes in this view' means the same thing in both places. It returns a 240-character preview instead of the body, puts pinned notes first, and fetches `limit + 1` rows to set an `X-Has-More` header without a count query. Named routes such as `/unfiled-count`, `/options` and `/tags` are declared before `/:id` so Express does not treat them as ids.

sections.title: Templates and saved views
sections.explanation: CRUD for the person's own templates (built-in ones live in the browser) and saved filter views. `cleanTemplate` validates and trims input, with a `partial` mode for PUT. Deleting a template or a view sends it to the recycle bin for 30 days rather than removing it.

sections.title: Ask your notes endpoints
sections.explanation: `POST /ask` is behind `aiLimiter` and calls `noteAsk.askNotes` (Step 8) with `routeDeps`. It stores each question and answer in `note_qa` with a trimmed source list, then deletes all but the newest 100 per person (`QA_KEEP`). Errors carrying a `.status` are passed through to the client, and anything else becomes a generic 500. GET and DELETE routes read or clear the history.

sections.title: Voice notes and conversations
sections.explanation: `personNames` collects the user's client, project and contact names as spelling hints. `/from-conversation` and `/:id/rewrite` only return proposals and save nothing. `POST /voice` writes the upload to a temp directory, converts it to a speech MP3 with ffmpeg, rejects long recordings (413), transcribes with Gemini, builds the note, and keeps the audio only if asked. A failure while keeping the audio never loses the note.

sections.title: Versions, to-dos, audio
sections.explanation: Version routes list, read and restore earlier versions; a restore first saves the current text as a version, so it can be undone too. `POST /:id/todos` turns to-do lines into tasks and marks the lines `{task:N}` without counting that as an edit. `PATCH /:id/audio/:attachmentId` changes how long kept audio stays.

sections.title: Single-note CRUD
sections.explanation: `clientIdIsOwned` and `projectIdIsOwned` check ownership by hand because `client_id` has no foreign key, and they send the 400 themselves. `PUT /:id` merges only the fields that were sent (older screens omit `client_id`), updates `updated_at`, queues an embedding refresh, may keep an earlier version, and syncs linked to-do tasks when the body changed.

sections.title: Filing endpoints
sections.explanation: Attachments, tags, reminders and pins are treated as 'filing', not editing, so they leave `updated_at` alone. Attachments reuse the shared upload policy (type checks, disguised-executable check, quota, at most 20 files). Reminders validate repeat rules and time zone, and marking a repeating reminder done moves it to its next time.

sections.title: AI action proposal
sections.explanation: `POST /:id/ai` is rate-limited and reads the saved note (the client saves first). It returns a proposal for summary, to-dos, tidy or title and changes nothing. Applying the proposal happens on the client through a normal save.

sections.title: Delete to recycle bin
sections.explanation: Delete runs in a transaction on a dedicated client: it locks the row with `FOR UPDATE`, collects tags and attachment ids, calls `bin.moveToBin` with the whole note as payload, then deletes the row. Attachments stay on disk so a restore can reconnect them. The `finally` block always releases the connection, and errors roll back.

server/services/modelResolver.js.overview: Decides which AI models a user can use. It reads the `vault_models` catalogue and `default_model` from settings (the user's own, otherwise the first admin with models configured), validates the catalogue, filters out non-text entries such as image or search providers, and picks tier slots (light, standard, plus per-provider defaults). There are no hardcoded model ids. Callers then pass the chosen id to callModel.js (Step 7).

sections.title: Catalogue validation
sections.explanation: `EMPTY_MODELS` is the null-everywhere result used whenever nothing is configured. `validateVaultModelsCatalog` checks before saving that the catalogue is an array and every entry has a non-empty `id`, and returns a list of invalid entries for the UI. Small predicates recognise image providers (`fal`, `seedance`, `replicate`) and search providers (`serper`, `serpapi`).

sections.title: Shopping search self-heal
sections.explanation: `ensureShoppingSearchModelInVault` appends a Shopping search entry to the first admin's catalogue if it is missing, and sets a default search provider. The promise is memoised in `shoppingEnsurePromise`, so this runs once per process; on error the memo is cleared so it can try again. It is a migration for existing workspaces, done lazily inside the resolver.

sections.title: Parsing helpers
sections.explanation: `isNonTextModel` excludes image, video and search entries by provider or id pattern so they are never picked for chat. The three `parse...` functions read the raw JSON setting defensively: invalid JSON or a non-array gives an empty list instead of an exception. They return ids only, `{id, provider}` pairs, or the full entries, depending on the caller.

sections.title: Tier selection
sections.explanation: `pickTiers` groups text models by provider, using explicit `provider` or id prefixes (`gemini-`, `deepseek-`, `ollama:`). `standard` is the configured default if it is in the list, otherwise the first model. `light` prefers local Ollama when `runtimeConfig.isLocal` and Anthropic first in hosted mode, falling back to `standard`.

sections.title: Settings resolution
sections.explanation: `loadFirstAdminSettings` groups admin settings by user and returns the first admin who actually has models, so an earlier admin with an empty list does not leave everyone without models. `resolveVaultModelSettings` uses the user's own catalogue when it is set, otherwise the admin's, and reports `fromAdmin` so the UI can explain where the list came from.

sections.title: Public resolvers and exports
sections.explanation: `getModelsForUser` returns tier slots and swallows errors into `EMPTY_MODELS`, so a settings failure means 'no model' rather than a crash. `getVaultModelsConfigForUser` returns the full catalogue and a valid default for pickers. `pickTextModel` walks a fallback chain that prefers standard or light, so callers do not each re-implement it.

server/services/callModel.js.overview: A single, provider-agnostic function for non-streaming text calls. Based on the model id prefix it sends the request to local Ollama (`ollama:`), Gemini (`gemini-`), DeepSeek (`deepseek-`) or Anthropic (everything else), and returns either plain text or `{ text, inputTokens, outputTokens, model, diagnostics }` for usage logging. It adds an optional timeout, image input for vision-capable providers, and Anthropic streaming for long outputs. Together with modelResolver and logUsage it forms the AI call path in Step 7.

sections.title: Contract and content helpers
sections.explanation: The JSDoc lists the options: `maxTokens`, `system`, `returnUsage`, `images`, and Anthropic-only `stream`, `onText` and `signal`. It notes that the SDK refuses long non-streamed answers, which is why `stream` exists. `normalizeMessageContent` flattens string or array message content into text, and `summarizeAnthropicContent` records block types and lengths for diagnostics.

sections.title: Timeout wrapper
sections.explanation: `callModel` requires a model id and, when `timeoutMs` is set, races the real call against a rejecting timer with `Promise.race`. The `finally` clears the timer so it cannot keep the process busy. The underlying request is not cancelled; the caller just stops waiting.

sections.title: Image check and Ollama
sections.explanation: `callModelInner` throws early if images are sent to a model that cannot see them (Ollama and DeepSeek). Ollama is required lazily and called with chat-style messages, and its token counts come from `prompt_eval_count`/`eval_count`. Empty replies are logged with a diagnostics object rather than thrown.

sections.title: Gemini branch
sections.explanation: Uses `@google/generative-ai` with the API key from an environment variable, passing the system prompt as `systemInstruction`. If `response.text()` throws (for example on a blocked or truncated candidate), it reads the parts by hand and records `finishReason`. An empty answer throws for normal callers but is returned with diagnostics when `returnUsage` is set, so callers like Product Scout can fall back.

sections.title: DeepSeek with retry
sections.explanation: Calls DeepSeek's OpenAI-style chat endpoint with `fetch`. The long comment explains a real failure: reasoning models can spend the whole `max_tokens` budget on hidden reasoning and return no visible text. When that pattern is detected (empty text, `finishReason: 'length'`, reasoning tokens at the budget), it retries once with a larger budget capped at 32768.

sections.title: Anthropic default branch
sections.explanation: Any other id goes to the Anthropic SDK. Images become base64 `image` blocks placed before the text. With `stream`, it uses `messages.stream`, forwards text deltas to `onText` inside a try/catch so a progress hook cannot break the call, and waits for `finalMessage()`. It joins every text block rather than reading `content[0]`, because newer models may put thinking or tool blocks first.

server/utils/logUsage.js.overview: A tiny helper that records one AI call's token usage and estimated cost in the `usage_logs` table, tagged by user, optional session, model and feature. Almost every AI feature calls it after callModel (Step 7), which is what powers the Usage & Cost page.

sections.title: Fire-and-forget usage insert
sections.explanation: Token counts are coerced with `Number(...) || 0`, and the function returns early when there is no user, no model, or zero tokens, so callers can pass results without checking. Cost comes from `calculateCost(model, in, out)`. The insert is not awaited and has its own `.catch`, so a logging failure never slows or breaks the AI feature that called it. A missing feature name is stored as `'unknown'`.

server/services/embeddings.js.overview: Turns text into embedding vectors and retrieves the nearest stored chunks for retrieval-augmented generation. The provider (Gemini in hosted mode, Ollama locally) and expected dimensions come from embeddingResolver, and vectors are checked against that size before use. `retrieveRelevantChunks` runs a pgvector cosine-distance query over `file_chunks`. MemoryService and noteAsk (Step 8) build on `embedText`.

sections.title: Gemini embeddings
sections.explanation: Input is cut to `MAX_CHARS` (30000). `embedWithGemini` tries the v1beta endpoint, then v1, moving on only on a 404 (model not on that API version); any other error is logged and gives `null`. The API key comes from an environment variable and is sent as a query parameter. It returns `null` instead of throwing, so callers treat 'no vector' as a normal outcome.

sections.title: Ollama embeddings
sections.explanation: Ollama is refused outside local mode. It tries the newer `/api/embed` endpoint (body `input`, reply `embeddings[0]`), then the older `/api/embeddings` (body `prompt`, reply `embedding`), so it works across Ollama versions. Each attempt is wrapped in try/catch and failures fall through to the next one.

sections.title: embedText entry point
sections.explanation: `embedText` resolves the per-user config, picks the provider, and discards a vector whose length does not match `config.dimensions`, because pgvector columns have a fixed size. It returns `sourceKey` (which model made the vector) only when a vector exists. Stored rows are tagged with that key so vectors from different models are never compared. `embedTextVector` is a legacy wrapper that returns only the array.

sections.title: Chunk retrieval
sections.explanation: The query vector is serialised as a pgvector literal `[a,b,...]` and cast with `::vector`. Rows are ordered by `embedding <=> $2`, the cosine-distance operator, and limited to `topK`. When a source key is known, only chunks from that model (or untagged legacy rows) are considered. Any error returns `[]`, so RAG fails soft and the chat continues without context.

server/services/MemoryService.js.overview: Per-user semantic memory stored in the `memory` table with pgvector embeddings (768 dimensions, per the header). It captures memories deduplicated by a SHA-256 content hash, updates, lists, searches by similarity, reports stats, backfills missing or outdated embeddings, and supplies relevant memories for a chat prompt. Every query is scoped by a validated user id. It builds on embeddings.js from Step 8.

sections.title: Validation helpers
sections.explanation: `normalizeContent` trims and caps text at 30000 characters, and `contentFingerprint` hashes it with SHA-256 for deduplication. `parseUserId` throws on anything that is not a positive integer, a cheap guard at the service boundary. `clampInt` bounds paging values, `rowToMemory` maps DB rows to a stable shape, and `embedForUser` returns the vector as a pgvector string literal.

sections.title: Capture with dedupe
sections.explanation: `capture` upserts on `(userId, content_fingerprint)`: saving the same text twice updates the row instead of duplicating it. Metadata is merged with JSONB `||`, and `COALESCE` keeps the old embedding if the new embed failed. The Postgres trick `(xmax = 0) AS inserted` tells whether the row was newly inserted or updated, which is returned as `created`.

sections.title: Update
sections.explanation: `update` re-hashes and re-embeds the new content and updates only a row owned by the user (`WHERE id AND userId`). A zero row count becomes 'Memory not found.', which also covers trying to edit someone else's memory. Metadata is replaced only when supplied.

sections.title: Search and list
sections.explanation: `search` embeds the query and orders by cosine distance, returning `1 - distance` as `similarity`. Results are limited to vectors from the current embedding source (or untagged rows), so vectors from different models are never mixed. If no vector can be made, it falls back to the newest memories via `list`, which pages with clamped limit and offset.

sections.title: Stats, remove, backfill
sections.explanation: `stats` counts total and embedded rows and reports memory health to SuggestionService in the background. `remove` is owner-scoped. `backfillEmbeddings` re-embeds a batch of rows that have no vector, no fingerprint, or a different `embedding_source`, which is how memories catch up after the embedding model changes.

sections.title: Prompt recall
sections.explanation: `getForPrompt` returns up to 12 memory texts for a chat message: semantically closest first when embeddings are available, otherwise the newest. Semantic failures are logged and fall through to the recency query, so chat always gets some context or an empty list, never an error.

server/services/noteAsk.js.overview: The engine behind 'Ask your notes' (Step 6, Step 8). A light model plans a search (keywords, dates, tags, client, project); Postgres full-text search finds notes and attached-file text inside an owner-checked scope, with wider and recent fallbacks; embedding similarity is fused with the word ranking when available; then the standard model answers only from numbered notes. The reply is cleaned so it can only cite notes and linked records that were actually supplied. Dependencies are injectable so the pure helpers and the flow can be unit-tested.

sections.title: Design notes and limits
sections.explanation: The header comment is the best map of the file: the Plan / Find / Answer stages, file text, hybrid search, linked records, and the security stance that note text is data and every query starts from the owner check in `noteQuery.buildFilters`. `LIMITS` sets per-mode budgets (detail: fewer notes with more text; overview: more notes with less), and `TOTAL_CHARS` caps the prompt. `STOP` lists filler words for fallback keywords.

sections.title: Plan sanitising helpers
sections.explanation: `normalizePlan` treats the model's plan as untrusted: known fields only, bounded keywords, validated dates (swapped if reversed), and mode restricted to `overview` or `detail`. `tsQuery` builds a Postgres tsquery from letters and digits only, so neither typed nor generated text can inject query syntax; words use prefix match (`:*`), phrases are joined with `&` and keywords with `|`. `dayStartUtc` uses the browser's time-zone offset, and `matchByName` maps a model-given name onto the person's real clients and projects.

sections.title: Fitting sources to budget
sections.explanation: `fitSources` numbers notes from 1, cuts each one to the per-note limit, and stops when the total budget runs low. It drops later notes rather than starving the first, highest-ranked ones. Matching file excerpts are added per note. `cleanHistory` keeps the last six user/assistant turns, trimmed, so follow-up questions work without sending unbounded history.

sections.title: Prompts and answer cleaning
sections.explanation: `PLANNER_SYSTEM` asks for a strict JSON plan; `ANSWER_SYSTEM` requires citations like [1], tells the model to treat note text as data, and forbids invented dates. `RELATED_RULES` is added only when linked records exist. `normalizeAnswer` removes any citation number or record key that was not supplied, a post-check that limits hallucinated citations. `describePlan` turns the plan into a short 'Looked for' line for the UI.

sections.title: Finding notes in SQL
sections.explanation: `TSV` weights title and tags above the body. `fetchRows` starts from `buildFilters` (owner check plus scope), then adds the full-text match, also searching attachment text, and ranks by `ts_rank_cd` with file matches weighted at 0.6. `scopeToQuery` turns the client's scope (all, current filters with a whitelist of keys, or one note) into a query, and `mergePlan` adds the plan's filters where the scope does not already set them.

sections.title: askNotes: find stage
sections.explanation: Validates the question, resolves dependencies from `deps` or the real modules, and wraps each model call to log usage. For one note it loads just that note; otherwise it counts the scope, plans with `models.light`, and falls back to plain keywords if planning fails. Plan tags, clients and projects are filtered to the person's own. Search then goes from planned filters, to a wider search, to the most recent notes. Embedding ranks are fused with word ranks (`fuseRanks`) on a best-effort basis, and missing indexes are backfilled in the background.

sections.title: askNotes: answer stage
sections.explanation: File text is loaded for the chosen notes, sources are fitted, and a `found` sentence tells the model how the notes were chosen (matched, wider, recent and so on). Linked records are gathered on a best-effort basis. `models.standard` writes the answer, which is cleaned, and an empty answer becomes a 502. The return value includes the sources with cited flags, the stage, and whether semantic search was used.

sections.title: Exports and test seam
sections.explanation: `routeDeps` is an empty object the route passes to `askNotes`; tests fill it with fake models and a fake pool. Exporting the pure helpers makes them easy to unit-test individually.

server/services/guideCore.js.overview: The shared engine behind the per-page AI guides (Step 9). A guide supplies a catalogue of its real controls, rules, unsupported actions and a system prompt; `createGuide` returns functions to build the prompt, clean the conversation, normalise the model's JSON verdict into a safe shape, and run the whole call with model resolution and usage logging. Model output is always treated as untrusted. notesTutor.js is one guide built on it.

sections.title: Purpose and shared helpers
sections.explanation: The header lists the four functions a guide gets and notes that some older guides still carry their own copies. `VERDICTS` is the closed set of reply types. `clip` collapses whitespace and bounds length. `cleanMessages` keeps only the last ten user/assistant turns, each capped at 1500 characters. `extractJson` accepts fenced or loose JSON by trying the fence, the whole text, then the outermost braces.

sections.title: Prompt builder
sections.explanation: `createGuide` builds an id set and a catalogue text from the guide definition. `buildPrompt` lays out the controls, rules, things it does not do, which tool is open, and the conversation. The screen context is clipped to 600 characters and explicitly labelled as information, never instructions, as a defence against prompt injection.

sections.title: Reply normalisation
sections.explanation: `normalizeReply` never throws. Unparseable output becomes a `question` verdict, using the prose only if it contains no braces. Steps are filtered to known tool ids, bounded to 8, and enriched with label and group from the catalogue, so the UI cannot show a made-up button. Verdict rules keep things consistent: `doable` needs steps, `partly`/`missing` need a `missing` text, and `beyond`/`question` carry no steps.

sections.title: The ask call
sections.explanation: `ask` requires the last message to be from the user (400 otherwise). It uses a model already validated by the route, or resolves the user's tier (light or standard, per `def.tier`), and returns 503 if none is set up. It calls the model with a 45-second timeout, converts errors with `modelCallError`, logs usage under the guide's feature name, and normalises the reply. `deps` lets tests inject fakes.

sections.title: Reply format constants
sections.explanation: `REPLY_FORMAT` and `VERDICT_HELP` are prompt fragments that each guide's system prompt includes, so every guide asks for the same JSON shape and verdict meanings that `normalizeReply` expects.

server/routes/guideRouter.js.overview: A factory, `makeGuideRouter`, that turns a guide's `ask` function into a POST endpoint (Step 9). It validates the optional requested model through the shared selection helper, calls the guide, and when the guide answers `missing` or `partly` it records the product gap once in the Suggestions inbox. It reads no files and writes no documents.

sections.title: Header and imports
sections.explanation: The comment states the contract: POST `{ messages, currentTool, context }` returns the guide's reply, and gaps go to Suggestions. Imports bring in Express, SuggestionService's `captureIf`/`makeFingerprint`, the request-scoped logger, and `resolveRequestedModel`, which is injectable through options for tests.

sections.title: Guide endpoint handler
sections.explanation: The handler bounds and type-checks body fields, then has `resolveModel` enforce the same model flag and id rules as other features. After the guide replies, a `missing` or `partly` verdict creates a suggestion whose fingerprint is built from the first 12 normalised words of the gap, so repeated asks for the same thing are deduplicated. That write is fire-and-forget. Errors with a `status` pass their message through; others get a friendly generic message and are logged under `logTag`.

server/services/notesTutor.js.overview: The Notes guide's knowledge (Step 9): a catalogue of every real Notes control with ids that match the client's notesTools.mjs (a test keeps them in step), the rules it may explain, what Notes cannot do, and its system prompt. It passes these to `createGuide` from guideCore.js and re-exports the resulting functions under Notes-specific names. The guide never sees any note content.

sections.title: Purpose header
sections.explanation: Explains what the guide does (points at real controls in order, or says plainly Notes cannot do it), that it never sees notes, and that its ids are shared with the client's tool list. It imports `createGuide` and the shared prompt fragments.

sections.title: Controls catalogue
sections.explanation: Each `CATALOG` entry has an `id`, `label`, `group` (Notes list, Editor, Chat and Notes), a plain-language `does`, and optional `notes` for limits. These ids are the only values `normalizeReply` will accept as steps, so this list is both prompt content and an allow-list. The detailed wording describes where each button is, for desktop and phone.

sections.title: Rules and limits
sections.explanation: `RULES` describes behaviour the guide may explain (autosave, voice notes versus dictation, to-dos becoming tasks only on request, the 30-day bin). `NOT_POSSIBLE` lists the gaps honestly (no OCR of images, no note sharing, no note links), which lets the model answer `beyond` or `missing` instead of inventing a feature.

sections.title: System prompt and wiring
sections.explanation: `SYSTEM` sets the tone and hard rules: use only the given tools, never guess note contents, one tool per step, and ask one question when unsure. It then appends `VERDICT_HELP` and `REPLY_FORMAT`. `createGuide` is called with feature `notes_guide` (the usage-logging tag) and a Notes-specific fallback answer, and the exports keep older names such as `askNotesTutor` for existing callers.

client/src/components/tutor/TutorChat.js.overview: The shared guide chat that every tool page reuses: a round button fixed at the bottom right that opens a small, draggable chat. The user asks what they want to do and the server returns a verdict plus ordered steps, each with an Open button that switches the page to that tool or tab. Pages never copy this file; they pass their wording and endpoint through a `config` prop. This is the client half of tour step 9, and it is wrapped in an error boundary so a broken guide never takes its page down.

sections.title: Imports and config contract
sections.explanation: Imports the API client, icon provider, voice input, drag hook, tooltip, auth store and model-name helper. The long doc comment is the real contract: it lists every `config` key (endpoint, payloadKey, verdicts, starters, wideKey, guideId, positionKey and so on) and the reply shape the server must produce (`{ verdict, answer, steps:[{tool,label,do}], missing, tip }`). It also notes the component must sit inside a VoiceInputProvider and that the guide only points, never acts.

sections.title: Reply rendering
sections.explanation: `historyText` flattens an assistant reply back into plain text so it can be sent as conversation history; the server sees prior answers as text, not JSON. `Reply` renders one structured answer: a coloured verdict badge looked up in `config.verdicts`, the answer, a numbered step list where each step has an Open button calling `onOpen(s.tool)`, a highlighted 'What is missing' note, and an optional tip.

sections.title: State, dragging and width
sections.explanation: `TutorInner` holds the chat state: open flag, input, busy flag and the `turns` array (user, assistant or error). Email panel state lives alongside. Two `useDraggable` instances let the button and the panel be moved, with positions stored under a key derived from `positionKey` or `wideKey`. The wide/narrow preference is read from localStorage inside try/catch because storage can be unavailable, and an effect scrolls to the newest message.

sections.title: Sending questions and emailing logs
sections.explanation: `send` appends the user turn, builds a `messages` array from user and assistant turns only (errors are dropped), adds the current tool/tab under `config.payloadKey` and an optional `model`, and POSTs to `config.endpoint`. Errors become an `error` turn rather than throwing. `emailLog` converts the turns into a neutral log and POSTs it to `/api/tutor-email`, then reports who it was sent to. Email is only offered after at least one assistant answer and when the page set a `guideId`.

sections.title: Collapsed launcher button
sections.explanation: When closed the component renders just the round graduation-cap button. `buttonDrag.guardClick` wraps the click so a drag does not also open the chat. The button merges the drag hook's handle props and position style with the theme colour.

sections.title: Panel and title bar
sections.explanation: The open state is a fixed dialog sized to 80% of the viewport height, using `dvh` where supported and clamped so it never exceeds the screen. The title bar is the drag handle (buttons inside it are excluded via the `ignore` selector) and double-click resets the position. It shows the guide name, the active model, an optional model selector (or a locked label when the admin chose the model), and buttons for wide/narrow, clear and close.

sections.title: Conversation list
sections.explanation: With no turns it shows the intro text and clickable starter questions that call `send(s)` directly. Otherwise each turn renders as a right-aligned user bubble, a red alert line for errors, or a bordered `Reply`. The container is `aria-live="polite"` so screen readers announce new answers, and the empty `endRef` div is the scroll target.

sections.title: Email this conversation panel
sections.explanation: A footer that starts as a single link and expands into checkboxes for 'Me' (showing the account email) and 'The admin'. Send is disabled unless at least one recipient is ticked; success and error messages use `role=status` and `role=alert`. Nothing leaves the browser until Send is pressed.

sections.title: Input box
sections.explanation: The composer uses the shared `VoiceInput` as a four-row textarea in append mode, so dictated text is added to what is already typed. Enter sends and Shift+Enter inserts a newline. The send button is disabled while busy or when the input is blank.

sections.title: Error boundary and export
sections.explanation: `Guard` is a minimal class error boundary: if anything inside the guide throws during render it switches to rendering nothing. The default export wraps `TutorInner` in it, which is how the tour's promise that a failing guide never breaks its page is implemented.

server/services/contractReview/contractS.overview: The data and access layer for Contract Review, written as plain exported async functions. It owns contract, party and document CRUD, starting and resuming reviews, promoting review results onto the contract, user corrections and obligation tracking. Every entry point goes through one access check, `assertContractAccess`, a deliberate single choke point. Tour step 10 uses it as the example of a larger tool keeping its logic in a service package rather than in the router.

sections.title: Header, imports and access error
sections.explanation: The header comment explains the design: functions instead of a class, and one central access check instead of the per-route owner checks used elsewhere. `ContractAccessError` carries `statusCode = 404`, so a contract you do not own looks the same as one that does not exist, which avoids revealing that it exists.

sections.title: Access checks and audit events
sections.explanation: `assertContractAccess` confirms the contract belongs to the user and is not soft-deleted, returning the `legalHold` flag for callers that need it. `assertDocumentAccess` does the same starting from a document id. `writeEvent` appends to `contract_events`, the audit trail, and takes a transaction client so the event commits or rolls back with the change it records.

sections.title: Contracts CRUD and soft delete
sections.explanation: Create, get, list, legal hold, title, review listing and CRM client links. `deleteContract` refuses while a legal hold is set and soft-deletes by setting `deletedAt`, because a hard delete would cascade away `contract_events` and destroy the audit trail. Inside one transaction it first unlinks any Tasks tied to the contract's obligations, appending a note to each task.

sections.title: Parties and role confirmation
sections.explanation: `addParty` records a party; `confirmParty` marks one party as the user. Because `isUser` must be unique per contract, the transaction clears it on every party before setting it on the chosen one, then writes a `role_confirmed` event. This is the step the analysis pipeline pauses for.

sections.title: Documents, quota and cascade delete
sections.explanation: Contract files are stored on disk outside the shared attachments table, so `assertContractDocsWithinQuota` sums their sizes itself and applies the same per-user quota (HTTP 413 when exceeded). `addDocument` hashes the upload with SHA-256 before storing it. `deleteDocument` removes a document and everything scoped to it.

sections.title: Starting and resuming reviews
sections.explanation: `startReview` validates access (and the optional 'review as another party' id), creates a queued review row and returns at once. Ingest, segmentation and `runAnalysis` then run in a detached async block, because OCR and several LLM stages can take minutes and a real incident showed long requests hitting infrastructure timeouts. The client polls `GET /reviews/:id` for progress. `resumeReview` uses the same fire-and-forget pattern for stages 5-11 after role confirmation. Modules are required lazily inside the functions, which avoids a circular import with `analysisPipeline.js`.

sections.title: Promotion and execution lifecycle
sections.explanation: `promoteReviewToContract` is the only path that writes contract type and key terms onto `contracts`. Contract-level corrections always win, amendments only promote fields they actually have, and a null never overwrites a known value unless a user correction set it. `markDocumentExecuted` supersedes other executed documents in the chain and promotes the review; `setContractStatus` only allows `expired` or `terminated`.

sections.title: Correction loaders and appliers
sections.explanation: Corrections are stored separately and never overwrite the model's output. Loaders read them in ascending order into Maps, so the latest correction per field wins. `applyPartyCorrections` returns an effective party while keeping `originalName`/`originalRole`. Clause and obligation corrections follow a carry-forward rule: they apply only if the current text still matches the snapshot taken when the correction was made, otherwise the item is flagged `correctedOnEarlierVersion`.

sections.title: Recording a correction
sections.explanation: `recordCorrection` allows at most one target (clause, obligation, party or definition) and looks each target up scoped to the caller's own `contractId`. The comment records why: an earlier version fetched by bare id, which let a user write another contract's data into their own corrections. It snapshots the matched text so the carry-forward check above can work later.

sections.title: Obligations, ICS export and clause search
sections.explanation: Obligation listing, tracked state, linking to Tasks, ICS calendar export and clause search, followed by the export list. `linkObligationToTask` refuses obligations whose effective verification status is `failed`, so a confirming correction is needed first. `syncObligationStateFromTask` is the one place where a Task points back: completing or reopening the Task flips the obligation's tracked state.

server/services/contractReview/analysisP.overview: Orchestrates Contract Review stages 3 to 11 once ingest and segmentation have produced clauses. `runAnalysis` runs type detection and party extraction, then either pauses at `awaiting_role_confirmation` or continues by itself; `resumeAfterRoleConfirmation` runs definitions, classification, risk scoring, obligations, summary and coverage. This is the multi-stage pipeline described in tour step 10.

sections.title: Header and stage imports
sections.explanation: The comment maps out which stages live here and which do not: ingest and segmentation run first in `ContractService.startReview`. Each stage is its own module (type detection, parties, definitions, clause classification, risk scoring, obligations, summary, coverage), plus a cost tracker, the prompt version and correction helpers from `contractService.js`.

sections.title: Fail loudly without a model
sections.explanation: `assertModelConfigured` throws a clear error when no Contract Review model resolves. The long comment explains why: each stage degrades quietly when it has no model, and the parties stage can still find names with a regex, so a workspace with no model would produce a plausible but empty review. One loud check at the start of each stage group replaces several silent ones.

sections.title: Status and context helpers
sections.explanation: `setStatus` builds a dynamic UPDATE that always sets `status` and `stageProgress` and can set extra columns, with every value parameterised. `loadReviewContext` joins the review to its document to get the extracted text, page map and contract id, and throws if the review is missing.

sections.title: runAnalysis: stages 3-4 and the pause
sections.explanation: Stamps the prompt version, then runs type detection and party/key-term extraction under a status update. If roles still need confirming and no explicit `asPartyId` was given, it returns `awaiting_role_confirmation` so the user can choose their side. Otherwise it starts `resumeAfterRoleConfirmation` without awaiting it, because stages 5-11 take minutes. Any failure marks the review `failed` with the error message before rethrowing.

sections.title: resumeAfterRoleConfirmation: stages 5-11
sections.explanation: A guardrail returns early for completed reviews, because later stages INSERT rather than upsert. It picks the user party (an explicit party for 'review as another party', otherwise the confirmed `isUser` party) and applies party corrections so edited roles really drive playbook selection. A contract-level type correction beats the detected type. The cost tracker is rebuilt from the persisted `costUsd`, since memory does not survive the pause. Each stage then runs in order before the review is marked `complete`; any error marks it `failed`.

server/services/recycleBin/index.js.overview: The shared recycle bin used across tools. A tool calls `moveToBin` inside the same transaction that deletes a row, and registers an adapter that knows how to restore that kind of item. Listing, restore, delete-forever, empty-bin and the 30-day purge all live here, so every tool behaves the same and no tool needs `deletedAt` columns. Tour step 10 uses it as the example of a cross-cutting service.

sections.title: Usage notes and limits
sections.explanation: The header comment is a two-step recipe for tools: call `moveToBin` at delete time and `register` an adapter once. Retention defaults to 30 days but can be changed with `RECYCLE_BIN_DAYS` (minimum 1). Payloads over 5 MB are refused rather than silently dropped. `RestoreError` carries an HTTP status, 409 by default.

sections.title: Registering adapters and moving to the bin
sections.explanation: `register` stores a `{ label, restore, discard }` adapter in a module-level Map; `discard` is optional and lets a tool clean up things the bin does not hold, such as uploaded files. `moveToBin` refuses unknown types, checks the JSON payload size (with a `maxBytes` override and a `TOO_LARGE` error code), and inserts the row with an `expiresAt` computed in SQL. Passing the transaction client as `db` makes the copy and the delete succeed or fail together.

sections.title: Purge and discard
sections.explanation: `purgeExpired` deletes expired rows and returns them so `discardAll` can notify each tool. `discardAll` is best effort: a failing adapter is logged and skipped, so one tool cannot block the bin.

sections.title: List, restore, delete forever, empty
sections.explanation: `list` purges first so the view is correct even if the schedule never ran, then returns up to 500 items with a computed `daysLeft`. `restoreItem` runs in a transaction: it locks the row with `FOR UPDATE`, rejects missing (404), expired (410) or unrestorable (422) items, calls the adapter's `restore`, and deletes the bin row only if that succeeds. `deleteForever` and `emptyBin` delete rows and call discard, always scoped to the user.

sections.title: Adapter loading and exports
sections.explanation: `loadAdapters` requires the `adapters` folder, whose files call `register`. The route and the scheduled job both call it so the registry is complete in either context. The internal `_adapters` Map is exported too.

server/cron/recurringCron.js.overview: The daily job that turns active `fin_recurring` templates into real draft invoices and expenses for the Finance tool. It runs at 00:05 behind `withCronLock` so only one container runs it during a rolling deploy, and processes each template in its own transaction. Tour step 11 uses it as the example scheduled job, and it relies on helpers exported by `routes/finance.js`.

sections.title: Imports and date helper
sections.explanation: Imports node-cron, the database pool and `withCronLock`. `addDays` and `daysInMonth` work purely in UTC on `YYYY-MM-DD` strings, which avoids local-time drift around midnight.

sections.title: Next occurrence with month anchoring
sections.explanation: `nextOccurrence` adds 7 or 14 days for weekly and fortnightly. Monthly, quarterly and annual steps are computed from an anchor day and clamped to the month's length, so an entry on the 31st goes Jan 31, Feb 28, Mar 31 instead of drifting to the 3rd for good. It is exported, which makes it easy to unit test.

sections.title: Finding due templates
sections.explanation: Today's date comes from Finance's `todayStr`, which uses the workspace timezone; the comment notes that UTC would date a morning run in Brisbane as the previous day. Each due template gets its own pooled connection and transaction, and takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock(7001, userId)`, the same per-user lock the invoice routes use, so invoice numbering cannot race.

sections.title: Creating a recurring invoice
sections.explanation: Reads payment terms from settings (default 7 days), finds the next `INV-<year>NNN` number, works out GST per line based on the user's registration on that date, and rounds every amount to cents. The invoice is inserted as a draft with its line items. Only `t.clientRef` is used, because the old client table was dropped and a backfill script repoints older templates.

sections.title: Creating a recurring expense with journal
sections.explanation: Splits the amount and GST depending on whether GST can be claimed; when the user is not registered, the GST becomes part of the cost. It then posts the same double-entry journal as a manual expense (debit Expenses, debit GST Paid, credit Bank) through Finance's `createJournalEntry`. The comment explains that without this the expense never reached the P&L or balance sheet.

sections.title: Advancing the schedule
sections.explanation: The next date is advanced from the scheduled date, not from today, so a late run does not shift the schedule, and periods missed while the server was down are skipped (with a 1000-iteration guard).
